content: 1. Health Financing Indicators: The budget allocated for implementing the national strategy on hearing care is often expressed as a percentage of the total health budget. This information is typically available in the financial planning documents and reports of the Ministry of Health. It can be calculated as: (Total amount allocated to ear and hearing care activities ÷ Total health budget) × 100. Similarly, the budget allocated for the office of the Ear and Hearing Care (EHC) coordinator can also be expressed as a percentage of the health budget using the same formula. 2. Per Capita Expenditure on Hearing Care: The per capita expenditure on ear and hearing care services, expressed in both national currency and US dollars, can be calculated as: (Total amount allocated to ear and hearing care activities ÷ Total population) × 100. This information is often found in Ministry of Health financial reports. 3. Health Information Indicators: Indicators for ear and hearing care should be included in the government-led health information system (HIS). These indicators should be collected and reported regularly. The inclusion of such indicators in the HIS allows for systematic monitoring and evaluation of ear and hearing care services. 4. Prevalence of Hearing Loss and Ear Diseases: The prevalence of hearing loss, expressed as a percentage of the population, should be disaggregated by severity, type, cause, age, and gender. This data should be collected at least once every 10 years through population-based surveys, including hearing tests and ear examinations. Similarly, the prevalence of ear diseases, such as otitis media, should also be assessed periodically using the same methodology. 5. Cochlear Implant Data: Records regarding the number and types of cochlear implants fitted in the country are often available with manufacturers. Discussions with health authorities can provide additional insights into the implementation of cochlear implant programs. 6. Policy and Legislation: Policies related to occupational noise control, hearing aid provision, and ototoxicity monitoring should be sought from relevant government departments, such as health, environment, and industry regulatory agencies. Legislation may also address hearing screening, hearing device provision, noise control, access to care, and recognition of sign language and alternative communication methods. 7. Human Resource Development: Information on the availability of qualified specialists, such as ENT specialists and audiologists, can be obtained from medical councils or national associations. Where such councils do not exist, government-approved organizations may provide similar data. 8. National and Subnational Reports: Reports from the Ministry of Health, hospitals, and implementing organizations should include data on ear and hearing care activities, such as hearing screenings, hearing aid services, and training programs. 9. Stakeholder Commitment: Stakeholders, including government and non-governmental organizations, should demonstrate commitment to ear and hearing care. Financial sponsors and other key stakeholders should be engaged to drive policy development and implementation. 10. Health Financing: The affordability of ear and hearing care services depends on government-led health financing schemes. 11. Health Information Systems: A functional health information system should include relevant indicators for ear and hearing care. 12. Educational Facilities for Training: Training facilities for health workers and professionals in ear and hearing care should be adequate to meet the needs of the entire country. Where facilities are insufficient, efforts should be made to expand training programs. 13. Monitoring and Reporting: Indicators should be carefully assessed for quality and clarity. Comparisons with other countries can provide valuable insights, but the basis for such comparisons should be clearly defined. 14. National Strategy Development: A national task force or committee should determine country-specific indicators based on the national strategic plan or existing ear and hearing care activities. 15. Regular Review and Recommendations: The national committee should regularly review data and provide recommendations to address gaps in ear and hearing care services. These recommendations should focus on policies, implementation, human resource development, and monitoring. 16. Comprehensive Reporting: A comprehensive report should document the status of ear and hearing care provision in the country. This report should include an executive summary, introduction, actions taken, indicators, comparisons, conclusions, and recommendations. 17. Annexes: Relevant policy documents, subnational reports, and other supporting materials should be included as annexes to provide additional context and detail.
